sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Our Madrid data is recent, so there is no city trend yet; the figures below are for weekdays and weekends in August and September 2026, which includes the August holidays.

Madrid's traffic rules have been rewritten twice in five years and fought in court throughout. In 2021 the Supreme Court rejected an appeal over the annulment of the ordinance articles that underpinned Madrid Central, the original low-emission zone, which kept issuing fines until that ruling became final [0]. The city replaced it with a wider 'Madrid 360' scheme in September 2021, which Más Madrid and Vox challenged in the regional high court [1]. A report of September 2024 said that court had annulled the parts of the ordinance defining the citywide zone, because the prior reports were insufficient [3]. In April 2026 the Supreme Court was reported to have refused to hear the city's appeal, leaving the annulment final. By then the annulled rules had been replaced by a newer ordinance [4], and the council approved Ordinance 2/2026 in March 2026 [5].

On the street, a January 2022 article described a dynamic tariff for the regulated parking zone (SER) that raises meter prices when nitrogen dioxide readings are high, with zero-emission vehicles exempt [2]. A December 2025 draft would extend the SER in phases to up to 22 more neighbourhoods, about 11,000 spaces by 2029 and a further 66,000 to 2035, with longer charging hours [6].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
EMT, the city-owned transport company, runs the municipal car parks directly, alongside private concessionaires [11], and earned €19.2 million from them in 2025 [13]. Its 2025 tariff decree sets maximum rotational tariffs, up to €38 for a full day [9], a 30% higher rate for the first four hours near venues holding more than 5,000 people during events [10], and free park-and-ride use of EMT car parks when the car stays 5 to 16 hours and the driver uses public transport during the stay [7]. EMT car parks may also apply tariffs that depend on a vehicle's environmental label [11]. The city approved the tender for a 25-year concession for three car parks on Calle Velázquez in 2023 [12]. In 2020 the regional transport consortium planned to add three EMT car parks to its park-and-ride network [8].

Charging has grown from a low base: 45 public fast chargers in 2020 [15], then 14 added at four central EMT car parks by early 2024, with plans for 33 new chargers across ten car parks, including those four [14]. The city publishes each EMT car park's total and free spaces by hour as open data [17]. Demand is strong: Metro carried a record 737 million trips in 2025 [18], fares are frozen for 2026 [19], and international visitors spent a record €17.9 billion [20].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Madrid's car parks are among the fullest in our set, and the gap between weekdays and weekends is small. The 23 we measure average 54% on weekdays and 52% at weekends, and use hardly rises or falls with distance from the Puerta del Sol: 51% within a kilometre, 56% between one and two, and 57–61% further out. Nearly all EMT car parks carry the same tariff in our data, €3.25 an hour and about €39 a day in the centre against €18–25 at the outer sites. With almost no price difference to compare, price tells us little about who parks where.

The fullest are the tourist centre's: Plaza Mayor (79%, 83% at weekends), Villa de París (74%), Pedro Zerolo (69%) and, on the edge, the Avenida de Portugal park-and-ride (72%) and the big Nuestra Señora del Recuerdo (832 spaces, 64%). The emptiest are Plaza de las Descalzas (16%) and Santo Domingo (29%). Some behave like commuter car parks (Marqués de Salamanca, 39% on weekdays and 24% at weekends), others like leisure ones, such as Sánchez Bustillo, which rises from 39% to 66% at weekends.
